clinicalPearls: A common anaemia arising in chronic infection, inflammation and malignancy, driven by immune activation rather than iron deficiency
Typically normocytic and normochromic, though it can become mildly microcytic in longstanding cases
The hallmark is functional iron restriction, with iron present in stores but unavailable for erythropoiesis
Ferritin is normal or raised while transferrin saturation is low, the reverse of the picture in absolute iron deficiency
The cytokine-induced hormone hepcidin blocks iron release from macrophages and reduces intestinal absorption
A low ferritin in a patient with chronic disease still indicates coexisting true iron deficiency, which should be sought
Management is directed at the underlying disorder, since correcting the inflammation improves the anaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Anaemia of chronic disease is driven by sustained immune activation. Inflammatory cytokines, particularly interleukin-6, stimulate hepatic production of hepcidin, the master regulator of iron. Hepcidin degrades the iron-export protein ferroportin, trapping iron within macrophages and enterocytes so that although stores are adequate the metal cannot reach developing erythroblasts, producing a functional iron restriction. In parallel, cytokines blunt the erythropoietin response and shorten red-cell survival, while direct suppression of erythroid progenitors further limits red-cell production. The net effect is a modest anaemia with high or normal ferritin, low transferrin saturation and raised hepcidin, distinguishing it from absolute iron deficiency in which stores are exhausted.
additionalDifferentials: Combined iron deficiency and anaemia of chronic disease
Anaemia of chronic kidney disease from erythropoietin deficiency
Anaemia from marrow infiltration or bone marrow failure
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film showing a normocytic or mildly microcytic anaemia
Ferritin, which is normal or raised in contrast to iron deficiency
Transferrin saturation and iron studies showing low saturation with low or normal total iron-binding capacity
Inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein to gauge disease activity
Reticulocyte count, typically inappropriately low for the degree of anaemia
Renal function and other tests directed at the suspected underlying disorder
redFlags: A disproportionately severe anaemia suggesting an additional cause such as bleeding or marrow disease
A low ferritin indicating coexisting iron deficiency that warrants investigation
New anaemia as the presenting feature of an occult malignancy or chronic infection
Rapidly progressive anaemia not explained by the known chronic illness
reference.prognosis: The anaemia is usually mild to moderate and follows the course of the underlying disease; it improves when the inflammatory process is controlled and rarely causes serious symptoms on its own.
pitfalls: Diagnosing iron deficiency on microcytosis alone without checking ferritin and saturation
Missing coexisting true iron deficiency when ferritin is low-normal in an inflamed patient
Giving iron indiscriminately when stores are already adequate but functionally locked away
Failing to pursue the underlying inflammatory, infective or neoplastic cause
management: Treat the underlying inflammatory, infective or malignant disorder, as controlling disease activity is the definitive route to correcting the anaemia
Identify and correct any coexisting true iron deficiency, indicated by a low ferritin, with iron replacement
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in selected settings such as chronic kidney disease, ensuring iron stores are adequate to support them
Intravenous iron preferred over oral when hepcidin-driven absorption blockade limits enteral uptake
Reserve red cell transfusion for severe or symptomatic anaemia rather than the modest anaemia typical of the condition
Monitor full blood count, reticulocytes and iron indices to track response and detect evolving deficiency
